summary_vn: Cách giải thích Tết với đồng nghiệp, hàng xóm, và bạn bè không phải người Việt.
summary_en: How to explain Tết to coworkers, neighbors, and non-Vietnamese friends.
regional_note: Phong tục Tết khác nhau giữa Hà Nội và Sài Gòn. Miền Bắc có hoa đào và bánh chưng vuông; miền Nam có hoa mai và bánh tét hình ống. Cả hai đều đúng — nói rõ vùng miền khi giải thích để tránh nhầm lẫn.

phrases.context: Lời chào đầu tiên khi gặp ai đó vào dịp Tết, cả qua tin nhắn lẫn trực tiếp.
phrases.english: I'm sending you Tết wishes — that's our Lunar New Year. Wishing you a healthy, lucky year ahead.
phrases.cultural_note: Tết is a multi-day national holiday in Vietnam, usually late January to mid-February. The greeting carries genuine weight — it's not a casual 'Happy New Year' equivalent.

phrases.context: Đồng nghiệp hỏi vì sao cần nghỉ phép.
phrases.english: Tết follows the lunar calendar, so the date shifts every year — it lands somewhere between late January and mid-February.
phrases.cultural_note: Most Western calendars don't show the lunar date, so coworkers genuinely don't know. Be specific about this year's Western date when asking for time off.

phrases.context: Giải thích phong bao đỏ cho hàng xóm hoặc đồng nghiệp.
phrases.english: We give red envelopes called lì xì — small amounts of money — to children and elders. It's about wishing them luck for the year, not the cash itself.
phrases.cultural_note: The amount is symbolic. New, crisp bills are preferred. The exchange is two-way: kids receive from adults, but adults also gift parents and grandparents.

phrases.context: Trả lời khi đồng nghiệp hỏi giá trị tiền trong phong bao.
phrases.english: The amount isn't the point — even a small new bill counts. What matters is the wish that comes with it.
phrases.cultural_note: Quoting amounts feels gauche in this culture. Steer the explanation back to symbolism.

phrases.context: Mời đồng nghiệp ăn bánh hôm nào đó vào dịp Tết.
phrases.english: This is bánh chưng — sticky rice, mung bean, and pork wrapped in banana leaves and boiled for hours. In the south we make a long cylindrical version called bánh tét.
phrases.cultural_note: Bánh chưng (square, North) and bánh tét (cylindrical, South) are not interchangeable in tradition — they map to different regional histories. Mention which one you grew up with.

phrases.context: Giải thích vì sao có cây hoa đào trong nhà dịp Tết.
phrases.english: In northern Vietnam, families display peach blossom branches at Tết. The pink flowers are believed to ward off bad luck for the new year.
phrases.cultural_note: This is a Northern Vietnam custom. Friends from southern Vietnam will display yellow apricot blossoms (hoa mai) instead — same purpose, different flower.

phrases.context: Giải thích cây hoa mai vàng trong nhà.
phrases.english: Down south we have yellow apricot blossoms — hoa mai. Yellow is the color of luck, so families compete to get their tree to bloom right at midnight on the first day of Tết.
phrases.cultural_note: If a Southern family's mai blooms early or late, that's a quiet disappointment — the timing matters. Don't joke about it.

phrases.context: Giải thích vì sao chọn người vào nhà đầu năm cẩn thận.
phrases.english: The first person to step into the house in the new year sets the tone for the whole year. Families pre-arrange a 'lucky' first-footer — someone with good fortune in their own life.
phrases.cultural_note: This is a serious custom in many families. Don't drop in unannounced on the first day of Tết — you might be 'taking' someone's chosen first-footer slot.

phrases.context: Mâm trái cây trên bàn thờ trong nhà.
phrases.english: We place a five-fruit tray on the family altar — the choice of fruits is symbolic. In the south, families often pick fruits whose names sound like 'just enough to use,' as a wish for sufficiency.
phrases.cultural_note: Hà Nội and Sài Gòn use different fruit selections. Ask before assuming what should be on the tray — there's no single 'correct' set.

phrases.vn_moment: Mùng một Tết cha, mùng hai Tết mẹ, mùng ba Tết thầy
phrases.context: Giải thích lịch thăm thân ngày đầu năm.
phrases.english: There's a saying: first day of Tết for father's family, second day for mother's family, third day for your teachers. The order matters more than people realize.
phrases.cultural_note: If your family follows this, plan around it. Skipping the order is read as disrespect even by relatives who would never say it out loud.

phrases.context: Câu nói khi đưa lì xì cho trẻ em.
phrases.english: When we hand the envelope, we say something like 'I wish you health, good grades this year, and that you grow taller than your mom.'
phrases.cultural_note: Wishes are personalised — not generic. Health and study come first; height and 'finding a good husband/wife' are common but optional.

phrases.vn_moment: Không quét nhà ngày mùng một
phrases.context: Giải thích vì sao không quét sàn ngày đầu năm.
phrases.english: We don't sweep the floor on the first day of Tết — there's a belief that you'd sweep your luck out the door with the dust.
phrases.cultural_note: It's not just a saying — many families genuinely won't pick up a broom that day. If you're a guest, don't offer to help clean.

phrases.context: Giải thích vì sao tâm trạng khi tiếp khách cần nhẹ nhàng.
phrases.english: We avoid arguing or saying anything heavy on the first day. Whatever happens at Tết is supposed to forecast the rest of the year.
phrases.cultural_note: Many topics are off-limits during Tết visits — money troubles, family fights, health diagnoses. Save the heavy conversation for after the holiday.

phrases.context: Giải thích vì sao xin nghỉ dài ngày để về quê.
phrases.english: Tết is the one time of year people travel back to where their parents live, even if it's a 12-hour train ride. It's the closest thing we have to a Western Christmas in scale.
phrases.cultural_note: If a Vietnamese coworker is requesting a full week off around lunar new year, this is what's happening. Treat it as non-negotiable family time.

phrases.context: Đồng nghiệp hỏi khi nào đi làm lại.
phrases.english: The official Tết holiday is around three days, but many families stretch it through to the seventh day of the lunar new year. After that, work resumes.
phrases.cultural_note: The seventh-day cutoff is a soft line — different families return to normal routines on different days. Don't be surprised if 'after Tết' means slightly different things to different people.

dialogues.title: Asking the boss for time off
dialogues.setting: You stop by your manager's desk a few weeks before Tết.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Hey, do you have a minute? I wanted to flag a holiday request for late January.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: It's for Tết — Lunar New Year. The exact dates shift each year because it's a lunar calendar holiday. This year it falls Jan 28 through Feb 3, and most Vietnamese families travel back home for it. I'd like to take that whole week if possible.

lines.speaker: Manager
lines.english: Got it — like a Vietnamese Christmas?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: That's a good comparison, yeah. It's the one time a year people travel back to their parents' hometown.

lines.speaker: Manager
lines.english: No problem. Send me the dates and I'll get them on the calendar.

dialogues.title: Coworker drops by your desk
dialogues.setting: A coworker sees the lì xì envelope on your desk.

lines.speaker: Coworker
lines.english: Hey, what's the red envelope? Looks fancy.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: It's a lì xì — a Tết tradition. Adults give kids a small amount of new bills inside a red envelope. The money is more about the luck-wishing than the amount.

lines.speaker: Coworker
lines.english: Oh nice. So it's like a Christmas card with cash inside?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Sort of — but it's not just kids. We give them to grandparents too. The wish goes both directions.

lines.speaker: Coworker
lines.english: That's a lovely tradition. Happy Tết, then.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Thank you — Chúc mừng năm mới.
